1.sense: The shortest surah in the Qur'an opens by telling one man that something has already been handed to him. The verb is in the past, so the gift is not promised or conditional, and the thing given is named with a word that means a great deal of something.

notes.t: Kawthar is built on the root k-th-r, much, in a pattern Arabic uses for the extreme of a quality. The word occurs once in the Qur'an and nowhere else in it, and it has no plural.

Anas ibn Malik reported that the Prophet ﷺ dozed briefly among them, raised his head smiling, and said a surah had just been sent down to him. He recited it, then asked whether they knew what al-Kawthar was, and said it is a river his Lord had promised him, on which there is much good, and a basin his community will come to on the Day of Resurrection.

Some of the early exegetes read al-kawthar more widely as every abundance given to the Prophet ﷺ, prophethood, the Qur'an, and his following, rather than the river alone. The report from Anas names the river, and the wider reading is offered as an addition rather than a replacement.
notes.src: the classical commentaries record both the river and the general sense

links.why: your Lord is going to give you, and you will be content, said to the same man
another short surah addressed to him listing what he was already given

2.sense: The gift is followed by an instruction, and the instruction is two acts of worship that cost something. Pray, and slaughter an animal, both of them done for the Lord who gave, which is the whole content of the response asked for.

notes.t: Li-rabbika, to your Lord, is placed between the two verbs so that it governs both. The prayer and the sacrifice are directed to one recipient, which is the point being made to an audience that offered both to other things.
Naḥara specifically means to slaughter a camel by piercing the naḥr, the base of the throat, as against dhabaḥa for sheep and cattle. The verse uses the more costly of the two.

The classical commentaries record more than one reading of wanḥar, chiefly the sacrifice, and also placing the hands at the naḥr during prayer, and facing the qibla. The great majority take it as the sacrifice, which the pairing with prayer and the parallel in Surah al-Anʿam supports.
notes.src: the classical commentaries record the several views; the majority read it as the sacrifice

links.why: my prayer and my sacrifice are for Allah, the same pairing said in the first person
neither the flesh nor the blood reaches Allah, but the God-consciousness from you does

3.sense: The surah closes by handing an insult back. Someone had called the Prophet ﷺ cut off, meaning left without a son to carry his name, and the verse returns the exact word to the person who used it, with the definite article added so that it becomes a title.

notes.t: Abtar is used of an animal whose tail has been docked, and then of a man with no male descendant and of anything left incomplete. The definite article on it here turns a description into the man's name.

The occasion reported is that a leading Meccan called the Prophet ﷺ abtar after his sons died in infancy. The reports name different men, al-As ibn Wa'il among them, and their wordings and chains differ, so the identity of the speaker is not settled even though the situation is well attested.
notes.src: reports collected by at-Tabari and Ibn Kathir name different men and differ in wording

notes.t: Shāniʾ is not the ordinary word for enemy. It names the one who feels hatred, from the root the Qur'an uses in Surah al-Ma'ida when it warns that hatred of a people must not push you into injustice.

links.why: the same root for hatred, there turned into a warning to the believers
he is not the father of any of your men but the Messenger of Allah and the seal of the prophets
